title: The s-passive: when nobody says who
goal: Understand and use the *s*-passive — *Kaffet serveras kl 8, Huset byggdes 1890* — and recognize it where Swedes use it most: on signs, in instructions and in the news.
bekal: the passive in four forms: *serveras, serverades, har serverats, ska serveras*
adding the doer with *av*, and saying it more casually with *man*
wave: Go back to Unit 4: say minnas, finnas and trivas in all four forms (minns – mindes – mints), then take your leave of an imaginary friend in three different ways — Vi ses! Vi hörs! Ha det så bra!

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Första kvällen på kursen

notes: **Kursen hålls här** — *hålls* (**hols**) is the passive of *håller*: "is held". The *s*-passive is built by adding *-s* to the verb, and in the present the *-er* or *-r* drops off first: *håller → hålls*, *serverar → serveras*. It's the same *-s* you met in Unit 4, now doing a third job.

**Kaffe serveras** — the passive lets you talk about an action without naming who does it. Somebody serves the coffee, but it doesn't matter who. If you do want to name the doer, add **av** (by): *Kaffet serveras av Lena.* In conversation that sounds stiff; Swedes would rather say *Lena serverar kaffet.*

**Dörren låses kl. 21** — a typical sign. Because *låsa* ends in *-s* already, the passive keeps an *-e-* to make it pronounceable: *låser → låses* (**LOH-ses**). The same happens with *läser → läses* (is read) and *kysser → kysses* (is kissed).

**Byggdes, renoverades** — in the past tense you simply add *-s* to the normal past form: *byggde → byggdes* (**BÜG-des**), *renoverade → renoverades*. Strong verbs work the same way: *skrev → skrevs*, *grep → greps*.

**Ska säljas, har diskuterats** — after a modal verb the passive appears in the infinitive (*säljas, göras, lösas*): *Skolan ska säljas*, *Det måste göras.* In the perfect, the supine takes *-s*: *har diskuterats, har bestämts*. **Nej då** is a friendly, reassuring "oh no, not at all".

**Två personer greps i natt** — classic news Swedish. *Greps* is the past passive of *gripa* (seize, arrest). Notice **i natt**: with a past verb it means "last night", with a present or future verb "tonight". Like *i helgen* in Unit 1, the verb decides.

grammars.title: Forming the s-passive
body: Take the active form and add *-s*. Only the present needs a little extra care: the final *-r* (group 1) or *-er* (other groups) is dropped before the *-s*.
after: Learn the passive by sound, not by rule: say *serveras, serverades, har serverats* aloud the way you'd say *serverar, serverade, har serverat*. The *-s* is pronounced clearly and never makes a new syllable — except in *läses, låses*.

Don't confuse the passive with the verbs from Unit 4. *Hoppas, finns, trivs* look passive but mean something active. *Serveras, byggdes, säljs* really are passive: something is done **to** the subject.

grammars.title: When Swedes use it — and when they don't
body: The *s*-passive belongs above all to **written, impersonal** Swedish. In everyday conversation people usually say the same thing actively, often with **man** (one, you, people).

after: Swedish has a second passive, built with *bli* + participle (*Hon blev inbjuden*) — that's Unit 6. For now, the *s*-passive is the one to recognize everywhere you look.

head: Sign
Meaning
rows: Please take your shoes off in the hall.
Tickets are bought in the app.
The laundry room is booked on the board.
Dogs must be kept on a leash.
Pay for your items at the checkout.
Dirty dishes go in the dishwasher.

blocks.text: The first sign is the most important one in Sweden. Swedes **always** take their shoes off indoors — at home, at friends' places, sometimes even at work. Walking into someone's living room with your shoes on is a real faux pas. Many hosts keep a basket of slippers by the door. Notice the particle verb in the passive: *ta av* → *tas av*. The particle simply stays where it is.

blocks.title: A recipe in the passive
items: *Ugnen sätts på 200 grader. Potatisen skalas och skärs i bitar. Allt blandas i en skål och bakas i 30 minuter.*
The oven is set to 200 degrees. The potatoes are peeled and cut into pieces. Everything is mixed in a bowl and baked for 30 minutes.
Older cookbooks are full of this style. Newer ones and food blogs mostly use commands instead: *Sätt på ugnen. Skala potatisen.*

blocks.text: Headlines and radio news love the passive because the event matters more than the person behind it. Learn to hear it and you'll understand much more of *Ekot* or *Rapport* — the main radio and TV news programs.

items: *Ny bro **öppnas** i Göteborg* — New bridge opens (is opened) in Göteborg
*Tre personer **skadades** i olycka* — Three people injured in accident
*Skolan **stängs** efter vattenläcka* — School closes after water leak
*Mannen **har gripits** av polisen* — The man has been arrested by the police

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 2
items: Combine a time clause with the passive: *När huset byggdes fanns det ingen hiss. Innan dörren låses måste alla gå ut.*
Check the word order in each main clause: the verb comes straight after the time clause.
